title: Sick on a journey
hook: Basho's last poem: sick on a journey, dreams wander withered fields (1694)
tomorrow: Issa lost his little girl. what two words did his poem end on?

segments.voice: That was the week from Tagore to Basho. Moments, and enough. Under the trees. What I have seen. The season word. Summer grasses. And yesterday's line: the narrow road. Now the last stretch of that road.
screen: `MOMENTS · UNDER THE TREES · WHAT I HAVE SEEN.` → `THE SEASON WORD · SUMMER GRASSES · THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: A trip cut short has its own ache: the fever on the last morning, the ride home early, the trail map with the end still unmarked. Basho's final journey ended something like that. In Osaka, far from his home, he fell ill, and his students gathered around his bed. From that bed came the poem remembered as his last: tabi ni yande, yume wa kareno wo, kakemeguru. Sick on a journey, my dreams go wandering over withered fields.
screen: `A TRIP CUT SHORT.` → `ILL IN OSAKA.` → `SICK ON A JOURNEY.` → `DREAMS OVER WITHERED FIELDS.`

segments.voice: Notice the season word, even here: kareno, withered fields, a winter word. The body lies in bed. The dreams are still out walking, over winter fields. A story his students told says that when someone asked him for a farewell poem, a custom among Japanese poets, he answered that any of his poems could be his last, because he had written each one as if it were. Here's the teaching, and it gathers up the whole week. Read with the Zen eye this week has followed, a journey isn't measured by whether it reaches the end. Each step was the road. Each poem was complete when it was written. Basho didn't finish wandering. His last poem doesn't mourn the unfinished road. It makes a poem of it, with the season in it. Now look back over the week. The butterfly that has time enough in moments. The school under the trees. Tagore's parting word of thanks. The season word that pins a moment as it passes. The summer grasses over the warriors' dreams. The road that was itself the home. Again and again this week, two poets made something whole out of what was brief, or broken off. So the trip that ended early, the plan that never got its last day, still counts as the road. Dreams wander, even over winter fields.
screen: `KARENO: A WINTER WORD.` · `EVERY POEM COULD BE THE LAST.` · `EACH STEP WAS THE ROAD.` · `ROOM FOR WHAT'S UNFINISHED.` · then, large: `DREAMS WANDER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one journey of yours that didn't finish: a trip, a plan, a visit you meant to make. Close your eyes and let your thoughts wander over it the way Basho's dreams wandered over the fields, without judging where it stopped. If you like, thank it for the part you walked.
Sick on a journey: the poem remembered as Basho's last, written ill in Osaka, with his dreams still wandering over withered fields.
Your line: dreams wander. The body rests, and the dreams keep walking the fields. Two weeks with the poets, done.
